title: "Is The Ratio of Normal Variables Normal?"
date: 2023-05-03
description: "Is a ratio of normal variables also normal? R simulations show when the approximation works and how the denominator can make it break down."
image: preview.png
image-alt: "Simulated ratio distributions: nearly symmetric when the denominator is far from zero, and right-skewed when it is nearer zero."
image-width: "1200"
image-height: "630"
open-graph: true
twitter-card:
  card-style: summary_large_image
categories: 
  - "r"
---

In _[Trustworthy Online Controller Experiments](https://a.co/d/b6Emaxo)_ I came across this quote, referring to a ratio metric $M = \frac{X}{Y}$, which states that:

> Because $X$ and $Y$ are jointly bivariate normal in the limit, $M$, as the ratio of the two averages, is also normally distributed.

That's only partially true. According to [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratio_distribution), the ratio of two uncorrelated noncentral normal variables $X = N(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2)$ and $Y = N(\mu_Y, \sigma_Y^2)$ has mean $\mu_X / \mu_Y$ and variance approximately $\frac{\mu_X^2}{\mu_Y^2}\left( \frac{\sigma_X^2}{\mu_X^2} + \frac{\sigma_Y^2}{\mu_Y^2} \right)$. The article implies that this is true when $Y$ is unlikely to assume negative values, say $\mu_Y > 3 \sigma_Y$.

As always, the best way to believe something is to see it yourself. Let's generate some uncorrelated normal variables far from 0 and their ratio:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(20230503)

ux = 100
sdx = 2
uy = 50
sdy = 0.5

X <- rnorm(1000, mean = ux, sd = sdx)
Y <- rnorm(1000, mean = uy, sd = sdy)
Z <- X / Y
```
:::


Their ratio looks normal enough:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hist(Z)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Which is confirmed by a q-q plot:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
qqnorm(Z)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


What about the mean and variance?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(Z)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2.000533
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ux / uy
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
var(Z)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.001997246
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ux^2 / uy^2 * (sdx^2 / ux^2 + sdy^2 / uy^2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.002
```


:::
:::


Both the mean and variance are _very_ close to their theoretical values.

But what happens now when the denominator $Y$ has a mean close to 0?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ux = 100
sdx = 2
uy = 10
sdy = 2

X <- rnorm(1000, mean = ux, sd = sdx)
Y <- rnorm(1000, mean = uy, sd = sdy)
Z <- X / Y
```
:::


Hard to call the resulting ratio normally distributed:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hist(Z)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Which is also clear with a q-q plot:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
qqnorm(Z)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


In other words, it is generally true that ratio metrics where the denominator is far from 0 will also be close enough to a normal distribution for practical purposes. But when the denominator's mean is, say, closer than 5 sigmas from 0 that assumption breaks down.
